KEY MESSAGE 1...Latest surface analysis this afternoon shows 
frontal boundary has cleared ENC and now sits offshore, leaving 
our area in partly cloudy skies. The front will help nudge 
temperatures down slightly compared to yesterday, felt most 
across the Albemarle Peninsula and northern Outer Banks with 
relatively cool onshore NW flow. Farther south and west, 
however, will see little relief as temps once again climb back 
into the mid 90s and Tds remain unrelenting in the upper 70s. 
Heat Advisory remains in effect for counties south of US264 into
this evening.

Boundary remains to our south for much of Sunday, but
temperatures have trended slightly lower tomorrow with likely
lingering convective debris and potentially earlier start of
convection. No Heat Advisories issued for tomorrow, although
spots from Lenoir County southward may get close to 105 for an
hour or two. Higher confidence in dangerous heat remains on 
Monday as the front lifts north and re- entrenches ENC in a very
hot airmass with 1000-850 mb thicknesses once again climbing 
above 1430m and widespread Tds in the mid to upper 70s. This 
could nudge max heat index values above 110 in many areas. We 
continue to encourage anyone planning on spending time outdoors 
to stay hydrated and to limit exposure to the heat, if able.

Another frontal boundary quickly pushes across NC on Monday 
evening before stalling along the coast. Like this weekend, SW 
counties will likely remain hot and humid while Albemarle and 
vicinity see some modest relief. A more widespread cooldown, 
however, is on the horizon late next week as a stronger cold 
front dives out of Canada and across the eastern CONUS.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Environment today once again appears at least 
marginally conducive for shower and thunderstorm development as 
ENC sits in northwesterly flow aloft and multiple mid-level 
disturbances rotate around a mid-level ridge stubbornly sitting 
over the Gulf States. Coverage today will be a touch better 
than yesterday, aided by sea and sound breezes as well as 
enhanced low-level convergence along the aforementioned frontal 
boundary. This most favors storm development, at least 
initially, along the southern coastline. Later in the day, 
upstream convection expected to develop in the NC Piedmont and 
southwest VA will migrate southeastward and potentially graze 
the coastal plain in the evening hours, although CAM consensus 
most favors areas west of I-95.

Pre-storm environment, like yesterday, is only marginally 
conducive for stronger storms with effective shear near 20 kt 
but ample instability forecast to reach 2500-3000 J/kg. An 
isolated wet microburst is possible, but a greater risk for 
stronger winds would be tied to more organized convective 
complexes likely to our west. Flooding threat today is more 
readily apparent - although storms will be somewhat progressive,
impressively high PWATs and sufficient saturation up to 500 mb 
point to highly efficient rainmakers easily capable of rainfall 
rates exceeding 2"/hr. Isolated flash flooding is possible, 
particularly for urban locations or those with known 
susceptibilities.

Frontal boundary begins to lift northward on Sunday, shifting 
more robust convection threat closer to VA but still leaving a 
favorable environment for sea breeze activity, as well as some 
upstream threats once again making their way towards the area in
the evening. Evolution will be heavily driven by mesoscale 
factors owing to continued higher than average forecast 
uncertainty owing to large spread in CAMs.

Another frontal boundary looks to approach on Monday. There 
will still be plenty of details to hammer out but both AI and 
trusted deterministic NWP guidance point to at least another 
marginal risk of strong to severe storms associated with this 
boundary. It will stall along our coast next week, keeping our 
area in an unsettled pattern through most of the work week.
